what: Red Rock Resorts runs casinos for Las Vegas residents. Its properties — Red Rock, Green Valley Ranch, Durango and others — are in the suburbs rather than on the Strip, and their customers are people who live in Las Vegas and visit regularly.
customers: Las Vegas residents who gamble, dine and use the amenities at its properties, typically visiting far more often than a tourist would.
money: Gaming revenue from slot machines and table games at its Las Vegas locals properties.
Restaurants, bars, hotel rooms, bowling and entertainment at the same properties.
moat: The locals business is structurally better than the Strip: a resident visits repeatedly, spends predictably and needs no airline ticket, convention or holiday to show up. Nevada gaming licences are limited and new casino sites in residential Las Vegas are constrained by zoning, which makes each property a protected local asset.
risks: Debt of $3.4B against $142.5M of cash is heavy relative to a $4.9B market value, and new property construction has added to it.
Free cash flow of only $50.8M against $116.7M of net income, because the company has been building new casinos — 97.0 times free cash flow.
Las Vegas's local economy depends substantially on tourism employment, so a downturn in visitation eventually reaches local wallets.
The shares trade at about 23.6 times earnings and 12.5 times EV/EBITDA.
Eighteen analysts average a $67.67 target against a $46.65 price, a 45% gap.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year, from $1.6B in 2021 to $2.0B in 2025.
The locals model produces repeat visits and predictable spending, unlike the Strip's dependence on travel.
Nevada gaming licences are limited and residential casino sites are constrained by zoning, which protects each property.
Las Vegas has been one of the fastest-growing American cities, which expands the local customer base.
Last year's net margin was 9.3%, solid for a capital-intensive casino operator.
watch: Same-store casino revenue and the performance of newly opened properties. The existing estate is the base; the new builds are where the capital went.
view: Red Rock is the purest expression of the Las Vegas locals casino model, and that model is considerably better than the Strip's. A resident visits regularly, spends predictably, and needs no airline ticket, convention booking or holiday to show up. Strip casinos depend on air travel, group business and discretionary travel budgets, all of which vanish together in a downturn. The locals business is closer to a neighbourhood amenity than a tourist attraction.

The asset protection is genuine. Nevada gaming licences are limited, and finding sites for new casinos in residential Las Vegas is constrained by zoning and land availability. Each existing property therefore has a defended catchment, and Las Vegas has been one of the fastest-growing American cities, which expands that catchment every year without the company doing anything.

What the company has done is build new properties, and that explains the financial picture. Free cash flow of $51 million against $117 million of net income, and $3.4 billion of debt against $142 million of cash, is a company that has been spending heavily on construction. That is the right use of capital if the new casinos earn their cost — a new locals casino in a growing suburb is about as predictable an investment as hospitality offers — but it leaves the balance sheet stretched while they ramp up.

At 23.6 times earnings and 12.5 times EV/EBITDA, the price assumes the new properties deliver and the leverage comes down. The eighteen analysts at $67.67 against $46.65 are modelling exactly that. The risk worth naming is that Las Vegas's local economy ultimately rests on tourism employment, so a sustained drop in visitation eventually reaches residents' wallets — the locals business is more insulated than the Strip, not immune to it. Same-store revenue and the ramp of the new properties are the two numbers.
bull: New properties ramp into a growing Las Vegas population while protected licences and zoning defend each catchment, and deleveraging lifts the equity.
bear: Tourism employment weakens and reaches residents' spending, new properties ramp slowly, and $3.4 billion of debt leaves no room for a soft year.
